title: My name is Lan
body: My name is Lan. I am ten years old. I live in Hanoi with my mother, my father and my little brother. We have a small house near a park. Every morning I walk to school with my brother. I like English and music. After school I play in the park.

title: At the café
body:
A: Hello. Can I have a cup of tea, please?
B: Sure. Would you like some sugar?
A: No, thank you. And one sandwich, please.
B: Cheese or chicken?
A: Cheese, please. How much is it?
B: Five dollars.

title: A weekend in the countryside
body: Last weekend, Tom visited his grandparents in the countryside. He took a train at eight o'clock and arrived at ten. His grandfather was waiting at the station with an old bicycle. They rode to the farm together. In the afternoon Tom helped his grandmother pick apples, and in the evening they cooked dinner. Tom was tired but happy. He wants to go back in the summer.

title: Train announcement
body: Good morning, passengers. The train to Hue will leave from platform 4 at 9:15, not from platform 2. This is fifteen minutes later than usual because of heavy rain. Please keep your tickets ready. If you need help, visit the information desk next to the main entrance.

title: Working from home
body: Many people now work from home at least some days a week. Supporters say it saves time on commuting and gives workers more flexibility. However, some employees feel lonely and find it hard to separate work from private life. A recent survey in a medium-sized company found that most staff preferred a mix: three days at home and two days in the office. Managers noticed that meetings were shorter, but new employees needed more help to learn the job.

title: Recycling programme
body: Welcome to City Radio. This week the council is starting a new recycling programme. From Monday, each home will receive three bins: blue for paper, green for glass and yellow for plastic. Collection will be on Thursdays instead of Fridays. Residents who need extra bins can call the council office before the end of the month. The council hopes the programme will reduce rubbish by thirty percent within a year.

title: Bees in the city
body: Urban beekeeping has grown rapidly in recent years, with hives appearing on the roofs of offices, hotels and even museums. Advocates argue that cities can offer bees a surprisingly rich diet, since parks and gardens flower over a longer season than farmland, where a single crop often blooms for only a few weeks. Critics, however, warn that an excess of hives may force wild pollinators to compete for limited food. Ecologists therefore suggest that planting more flowers, rather than adding more hives, would benefit both honeybees and wild species.

title: Sleep and memory
body: Today I'd like to talk about sleep and memory. Many students believe that staying up all night to study is effective, but research suggests otherwise. During sleep, the brain organises what we have learned during the day and moves important information into long-term memory. In one experiment, two groups learned the same list of words. The group that slept for eight hours remembered about forty percent more than the group that stayed awake. So the best advice is to study in the evening and sleep well, rather than cram.

title: The productivity paradox
body: The notion that technology inevitably boosts productivity has been challenged by economists who point to the so-called productivity paradox: despite massive investment in computers since the 1980s, measurable gains in output were slow to appear. One explanation is that new tools demand organisational change before they pay off; firms that merely automated old procedures saw little benefit, whereas those that redesigned workflows reaped substantial returns. Others argue that official statistics fail to capture improvements in quality, such as better software or free online services, which do not show up as higher sales. Whichever view is correct, the episode suggests that the effect of any innovation depends less on the invention itself than on how people choose to use it.

title: Car-free streets
body: Good evening and welcome to the Architecture Society's annual talk. Tonight's speaker, an urban planner, will discuss why many modern cities are rediscovering the humble pedestrian street. Rather than seeing car-free zones as a threat to shops, planners increasingly view them as an opportunity: studies from several European capitals indicate that footfall rises and local businesses gain once traffic is removed. Of course, success depends on good public transport, and cities that closed roads without improving buses and trams met fierce opposition. The talk begins at seven thirty in the main hall, and questions will be taken at the end.
